summary: This is an April 1st joke RFC. It defines the NSA (No Secrecy Afforded) certificate extension for X.509 certificates, a satirical way to say that private keys may no longer be secret. It is not a serious specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a joke document about a certificate that admits a secret key is no longer secret. It pokes fun at spying worries.

subtitle: A satirical certificate extension for compromised keys

tldr.problem: This is an April 1st joke RFC. It humorously addresses the reality that sometimes private keys are compromised or must be shared with authorities.
tldr.mechanism: It defines the NSA (No Secrecy Afforded) certificate extension, a boolean flag in X.509 certificates that indicates whether a private key has been shared with a third party.
tldr.outcome: The RFC uses dark humor to make a point about security: if keys are compromised, better to say so explicitly than hide it. The joke parodies surveillance and cryptographic vulnerability.

today: RFC 7169 is an April Fools' Informational document and has not been obsoleted. It remains a humorous take on the real problem of key compromise.

sections.title: The NSA Extension
sections.content:
This is an April 1st RFC published as informational. It humorously defines the NSA (No Secrecy Afforded) certificate extension for use in X.509 public key certificates. The title is a play on words: NSA stands both for the U.S. National Security Agency and for "No Secrecy Afforded."

The document addresses a real problem: sometimes private keys are shared with third parties due to law enforcement demands, system compromises, or other circumstances. The joke proposes that entities should openly declare this compromise rather than hide it.
sections.plainLanguage: This April Fools joke says that if your secret key is not secret anymore, you should put a label on your certificate admitting it.

sections.title: How the Extension Works
sections.content: The extension uses a simple boolean flag in the certificate. Setting it to TRUE means the key has definitely been shared with a third party. Setting it to FALSE means the key may have been shared, but the signer chooses not to openly declare it. The extension is always marked critical, forcing relying parties to notice it and make an explicit security decision.
sections.plainLanguage: The flag is either 'yes this key is compromised' or 'maybe it is, who knows.' Either way, the relying party has to think about it.

sections.title: Serious Implications
sections.content: The RFC notes, tongue-in-cheek, that keys with this extension require careful trust decisions. The security considerations section advises that lengthy deliberations about whether to trust the keys are necessary, and rushing a security analysis is never wise. Ultimately, the keys may not be trusted at all. The closing line sums up the joke: "Secrecy is hard."
sections.plainLanguage: If a key admits it is compromised, you should think hard before trusting it. You can just decide not to.

references.text: Cooper, D., Santesson, S., Farrell, S., Boeyen, S., Housley, R., and W. Polk, "Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and Certificate Revocation List (CRL) Profile", RFC 5280, May 2008.
